insights.headline: South Sudan conflict intensity tracks global copper prices, not the other way around
insights.detail: Conflict events, protest events, and severity in South Sudan all correlate strongly (r ~0.5-0.7) with copper, silver, gold, platinum, and aluminum prices, with zero lag and consistent across nearly every conflict metric. This pattern looks less like conflict driving metal prices and more like both being driven by a common global commodity super-cycle or dollar-liquidity regime that also finances armed groups and state security spending in resource-linked economies. For investors, a broad-based global metals rally could be a leading indicator to tighten risk monitoring on South Sudan exposure, since periods of high commodity prices historically coincide with elevated internal conflict there.
insights.caveat: The most likely confounder is a common global macro factor (dollar weakness, global growth, China demand) driving all base/precious metal prices simultaneously, which would produce this same correlation pattern across every metal regardless of any real causal link to South Sudan's conflict; it is not evidence that South Sudanese conflict moves world copper markets.

insights.headline: Mozambique conflict/violence leads copper prices by up to a month
insights.detail: Mozambique's conflict events, political violence, and severity metrics correlate with copper both contemporaneously and with a 1-month lag (r ~0.69-0.72). Mozambique has real copper-adjacent mining and gas infrastructure exposure (Cabo Delgado insurgency near gas projects), so this could reflect investor risk repricing of regional supply disruption, or simply mirror the same global copper cycle seen elsewhere. Still, if the lagged relationship holds out-of-sample, a spike in Mozambican political violence could be a short-horizon signal to watch regional mining/gas equities and country risk premia.
insights.caveat: With only 18-19 monthly observations, this could easily be a chance alignment of two series that both moved during the same global commodity upswing; reverse causality is also plausible if rising copper prices increase the value of contested resource areas and thereby fuel local conflict, rather than conflict driving price.

insights.headline: Kenyan conflict, protest, and political violence all predict a rise in investment activity three months later
insights.detail: Three separate Kenyan instability measures (conflict events, protest events, political violence events) each correlate at r=0.575 with investment_events three months later, over a much larger sample (63 months) than most other findings here. A plausible story: instability spikes trigger post-crisis stabilization and reconstruction financing, or election-cycle unrest is followed by renewed donor/investor confidence once the cycle resolves, both of which are common in Kenya's political calendar. This is genuinely useful for entry-timing: rather than treating unrest as a pure risk-off signal, the data suggest development-finance flows into Kenya often resume a quarter after unrest, which could inform re-entry timing for frontier-market allocators.
insights.caveat: The three instability series are highly collinear with each other (identical r and lag), so this is really one signal, not three independent confirmations; election-cycle seasonality is a likely confounder, since both unrest and investment announcements may cluster around Kenya's fixed election calendar rather than being causally linked.

insights.headline: South Sudan investment activity leads aluminum prices by three months
insights.detail: South Sudan's investment_events series correlates with aluminum prices at r=0.615 with a 3-month lag, distinct from the contemporaneous conflict-metal correlations. Because South Sudan is not a major aluminum producer, this is more likely investment activity responding to (or co-moving with) the same global capital-flow/risk-appetite cycle that later shows up in industrial metal prices, rather than a direct local supply link. It's a marginal, secondary signal worth tracking only in combination with broader emerging-market capital flow data, not as a standalone aluminum trade idea.
insights.caveat: A global risk-on/risk-off cycle in emerging-market capital flows could independently drive both frontier-market investment announcements and industrial metal demand, producing this lagged correlation without any direct causal channel between South Sudanese investment and aluminum specifically.
